title: In utero reversal of placental insufficiency

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment that reverses established placental insufficiency while pregnancy continues. The placenta would recover enough of its ability to support fetal growth and development that placental disease no longer requires early delivery. In pregnancies with preeclampsia, treatment would also need to resolve the associated maternal endothelial syndrome—the dysfunction of blood-vessel lining that contributes to maternal illness. These are connected but distinct targets: isolated placental fetal growth restriction need not include a maternal endothelial syndrome.

The intended scope is placental insufficiency underlying early preeclampsia or placental fetal growth restriction. It does not encompass every cause of fetal growth restriction, chronic hypertension, or every hypertensive disorder of pregnancy. Its defining advance would be disease modification after placental disease has begun, beyond preventing some cases, controlling blood pressure or seizures, or changing a circulating biomarker. The supplied evidence does not demonstrate that this capability has been achieved.

significance.text: The 2023 reviews describe delivery as the only definitive cure for preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction. When severe placental disease develops early, delivery can exchange the risks of continued pregnancy for the risks of serious prematurity. Safely reversing the disease in utero would introduce a fundamentally different option: treating the dysfunctional placenta in place while allowing pregnancy to continue. Avoiding otherwise indicated early delivery would follow directly from a successful demonstration of that capability.

Preeclampsia is a leading cause of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality, and fetal growth restriction is associated with adverse outcomes before and after birth. A successful treatment could reduce maternal crises, improve fetal growth, and reduce harm associated with prematurity. Those benefits, and their magnitude, would need to be measured in clinical studies; extra time in pregnancy is valuable only if maternal and fetal health remain sufficiently protected.

The potential impact has important boundaries. Survivors of preeclampsia have increased later cardiovascular risk, but the supplied evidence does not establish preeclampsia as a leading cause of later cardiovascular disease or show that reversing the pregnancy syndrome would prevent that later disease. Similarly, delivery ends dependence on the dysfunctional placenta without necessarily immediately resolving maternal illness or reversing fetal injury already sustained. An in-utero treatment would need separate evidence for durable maternal and child benefits.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is coordinated recovery of placental support for the fetus and, where present, resolution of maternal disease after onset. Human preeclampsia has an incompletely defined aetiology. A dysfunctional placenta releases factors that contribute to maternal endothelial dysfunction, including the antiangiogenic factor soluble Fms-like tyrosine kinase-1, or sFlt-1. Identifying a contributor to maternal illness does not establish that removing it repairs the placental processes responsible for inadequate fetal support.

The 2026 selective sFlt-1 removal pilot illustrates this distinction. It reported changes in circulating sFlt-1 and maternal blood pressure, but the supplied abstract does not establish restored placental exchange, normalized fetal growth, resolution of the whole maternal syndrome, or safe continuation to term. Its findings cannot settle whether every possible strategy targeting an antiangiogenic signal would succeed or fail.

Engineering synthesis: a convincing therapy must connect a biological intervention to sustained organ function and clinical safety. Concrete barriers include determining which established placental injuries remain reversible, identifying pregnancies likely to respond, distinguishing improvement in maternal circulating signals from recovery of fetal support, and maintaining benefit without exposing the mother or fetus to unacceptable treatment risks. Different presentations may require different interventions; a treatment effective for one placental disease subgroup would not establish efficacy across all placental insufficiency.

current_state.text: Dimitriadis and colleagues’ review, published on 16 February 2023 in Nature Reviews Disease Primers, describes treatment directed at hypertension and seizures while identifying delivery of the placenta and baby as the only definitive cure for preeclampsia, often at a premature gestation. Giouleka and colleagues’ November 2023 review of major fetal-growth-restriction guidelines in Obstetrical & Gynecological Survey likewise describes delivery as the only definitive cure. These are dated descriptions of the therapeutic gap, rather than proof of treatment availability or absence at every subsequent date.

Prevention has demonstrated efficacy in a defined population. In Rolnik and colleagues’ 2017 randomized aspirin-versus-placebo trial in pregnancies screened as high risk, treatment began at 11–14 weeks and continued until 36 weeks. Preterm preeclampsia occurred in 13 participants receiving aspirin, or 1.6%, compared with 35 receiving placebo, or 4.3%; the reported odds ratio was 0.38. Disease still occurred, and the trial addressed prevention before onset rather than reversal of established placental disease.

Thadhani and colleagues’ 2026 Nature Medicine report describes an investigational, single-arm, open-label pilot of selective sFlt-1 removal by apheresis in very preterm preeclampsia, with safety and tolerability as its primary endpoints. In the nine-person multiple-dose phase B cohort, each apheresis reduced sFlt-1 by 16.7 ± 7.6% and mean arterial pressure by 4.1 ± 7.8 mmHg. Pregnancy continued from admission for a median of 10 days, with a range of 3–19 days. These quantitative findings apply to that phase B cohort and should not be generalized to all pilot participants.

The observed time from admission to delivery is not a demonstrated treatment-attributable extension of pregnancy: the uncontrolled design cannot establish how long those pregnancies would otherwise have continued. The pilot supports further investigation of selective sFlt-1 removal, and its authors call for controlled trials to assess additional safety and efficacy. It does not establish reversal that removes the need for disease-driven early delivery, normalized fetal growth, or safe continuation to term.

Evidence-access limitation: the supplied review assessed abstracts rather than the complete articles for all four sources. The aspirin URL requested full text but resolved to an abstract page. The retained pages were reported as untruncated and without extraction issues, but that does not make them complete article texts; detailed methods and outcomes beyond the reviewed abstracts cannot be assumed.

Evidence-coverage limitation: although the source index records retrieval on 1 November 2026, the supplied material contains no bounded freshness search establishing that these were the latest results or that no qualifying treatment was available through that date. The record therefore documents a therapeutic gap in the 2023 reviews and an investigational approach in 2026, while leaving the exhaustive present-day availability question unresolved. This limitation does not invalidate the reported dated findings.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: enroll pregnancies with clearly defined early-onset preeclampsia or severe early fetal growth restriction attributable to placental insufficiency, and compare a prespecified treatment with a concurrent control. The study should demonstrate sustained recovery of placental support and fetal growth, resolution of maternal disease when present, and continuation into a prespecified gestational range associated with substantially less serious prematurity. The goal is to remove the placental disease indication for early delivery within the demonstrated population; reaching term need not be the only meaningful endpoint.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained placental recovery removes disease indication for early delivery

completion_criteria.text: Proposed safety and efficacy requirements: define numerical gestational targets, fetal-growth and maternal-disease endpoints, acceptable safety margins, rescue-delivery rules, follow-up periods, and adequate statistical power before testing. Benefit should not come with an unacceptable increase in stillbirth, maternal organ failure, or serious neonatal harm. A biomarker reduction, modest blood-pressure change, or a few observed additional days in a single-arm study would not by itself demonstrate disease reversal.
completion_criteria.label: Numerical efficacy targets and safety margins defined before testing

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: confirm benefit across independent studies or centers, characterize response by gestational age and placental disease presentation, and establish a treatment schedule that can be delivered safely during pregnancy. Follow-up should assess whether maternal recovery persists and whether children benefit beyond delayed delivery. These are proposed criteria, not established consensus standards. Finite trials would establish demonstrated efficacy and safety within their studied populations, rather than universal reversibility of placental insufficiency.
completion_criteria.label: Independent studies confirm benefit and define safe treatment schedules

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OBG-01, Causal control of the human parturition clock, overlaps in the aim of extending pregnancy. Its target is the timing of labor; OBG-04 targets placental dysfunction that can require delivery even when spontaneous labor has not begun. Suppressing labor would not itself establish restored placental support or resolution of maternal disease.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-10, Restoration of the amniotic compartment after preterm membrane rupture, addresses another route to premature birth. Repairing membranes or restoring the amniotic compartment would not itself repair placental exchange, while placental recovery would not demonstrate membrane repair. Both capabilities could matter in a pregnancy with more than one complication, but they require distinct demonstrations.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-03, Extrauterine physiological support across the viability gap, shares the goal of reducing harm when pregnancy cannot continue safely. OBG-03 concerns support outside the uterus; OBG-04 seeks to preserve a safe intrauterine pregnancy by reversing the placental disease that would otherwise prompt delivery. Success in either would not establish the other.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-06, In utero molecular correction of fetal-onset genetic disease, also proposes treatment before birth, but targets a molecular cause of fetal disease. OBG-04 targets the placenta and associated maternal illness. Improved fetal growth after placental treatment would not demonstrate correction of a fetal genetic disorder.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-08, A manufactured uterus that supports pregnancy without a donor graft and chronic immunosuppression, overlaps in the broader challenge of sustaining gestation. Its defining capability is a manufactured uterine environment; OBG-04 concerns recovery of a dysfunctional placenta during an existing pregnancy. Neither capability implies the other.

Aspirin prevention is a relevant clinical comparator rather than an equivalent breakthrough. The supplied randomized trial demonstrates reduced preterm preeclampsia incidence in screened high-risk pregnancies when treatment begins before disease onset. OBG-04 requires treatment after placental disease has become established. Prevention remains clinically valuable, but it answers a different therapeutic question.

change_log.change: Preserved OBG-04 and its title while defining reversal as recovery of placental fetal support and resolution of maternal disease when present.
change_log.reason: This retains the innovation’s identity while distinguishing isolated placental fetal growth restriction from preeclampsia with a maternal endothelial syndrome.

change_log.change: Restricted fetal-growth-restriction scope to placental causes and distinguished chronic hypertension and other hypertensive disorders.
change_log.reason: Fetal growth restriction has heterogeneous causes, and the proposed placental intervention does not imply treatment of every growth or blood-pressure disorder.

change_log.change: Replaced an exhaustive claim about failed antiangiogenic blockade with the specific findings and limits of selective sFlt-1 removal.
change_log.reason: The pilot does not test all signal-blocking strategies or establish restored placental exchange or safe continuation to term.

change_log.change: Specified that the 2026 quantitative results concern the nine-person multiple-dose phase B cohort and added the reported blood-pressure change.
change_log.reason: The review supports cohort-specific reductions of 16.7 ± 7.6% in sFlt-1 and 4.1 ± 7.8 mmHg in mean arterial pressure.

change_log.change: Distinguished the median 10-day observed continuation from treatment-attributable pregnancy prolongation.
change_log.reason: A single-arm study lacks the concurrent comparison needed to establish causal extension.

change_log.change: Corrected the later cardiovascular claim to increased risk and separated possible long-term benefit from demonstrated outcomes.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not support a leading-cause ranking or establish that treating the pregnancy syndrome prevents later cardiovascular disease.

change_log.change: Clarified that delivery does not necessarily immediately resolve all maternal illness or reverse fetal consequences.
change_log.reason: Ending dependence on the dysfunctional placenta is distinct from complete recovery from its effects.

change_log.change: Preserved the aspirin trial’s event counts, rates, odds ratio, and treatment timing while distinguishing prevention from reversal.
change_log.reason: The randomized evidence concerns screened high-risk pregnancies treated before disease onset.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to include reproducibility, prespecified outcomes, safety boundaries, rescue delivery, follow-up, and population limits.
change_log.reason: These details make a convincing demonstration assessable without presenting proposed criteria as established standards.

change_log.change: Retained abstract-access and freshness limitations and separated them from the validity of dated findings.
change_log.reason: Complete retained webpages are not complete articles, and retrieval dates do not establish an exhaustive search through 1 November 2026.

change_log.change: Integrated relevant roster distinctions and labeled unsourced engineering reasoning and proposed demonstrations explicitly.
change_log.reason: This preserves related concepts as separate entries and distinguishes source-backed findings from synthesis.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record does not establish whether a qualifying treatment remained unavailable through 1 November 2026; no bounded freshness search was supplied.

Full article methods and outcomes were not available in the reviewed evidence. The abstract-level record cannot resolve additional details of participant selection, safety, fetal outcomes, or follow-up.
It remains unresolved whether selective sFlt-1 removal produces sustained placental recovery or clinically meaningful benefits beyond the biochemical and blood-pressure changes reported in the pilot.
Which placental disease subtypes and stages remain reversible, and whether maternal and fetal responses can be restored together, remain open questions.

Numerical gestational targets, disease-resolution definitions, fetal-growth endpoints, safety margins, sample sizes, and follow-up durations remain to be specified for an actual demonstration protocol.
Any effect of successful in-utero reversal on later maternal cardiovascular disease or long-term child health would require separate evidence.

brief.title: Repairing the placenta during pregnancy
possible: A pregnancy threatened by a failing placenta—the organ that supports the growing baby—could continue safely after treatment restores its function. For early preeclampsia, a pregnancy illness involving high blood pressure and other complications, treatment would also resolve the mother's illness.
why: Families facing severe placental disease early in pregnancy could gain an option beyond early delivery. Restoring the placenta could improve the baby's growth, reduce maternal crises and avoid harm from being born too soon.

sources.showed: Their review described how a dysfunctional placenta causes maternal illness in preeclampsia. It identified delivery as the only cure, with available treatments targeting blood pressure and seizures.
sources.cited_for: The review explains why treating maternal symptoms alone does not reverse placental disease.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate a treatment that restores placental function during pregnancy.

sources.showed: Their review compared guidelines for fetal growth restriction, when a baby grows too slowly before birth. It found agreement on some aspects of care but differences in definitions and monitoring.
sources.quote: Several discrepancies were identified regarding the definition of FGR and small-for-gestational-age fetuses, the diagnostic criteria, and the need of testing for congenital infections.
sources.cited_for: The review describes delivery as the only definitive cure for fetal growth restriction.
sources.not_established: The review does not show that treatment can restore growth by repairing the placenta.

sources.showed: A randomized trial found that low-dose aspirin reduced preeclampsia requiring early delivery in pregnancies screened as high risk.
sources.quote: Treatment with low-dose aspirin in women at high risk for preterm preeclampsia resulted in a lower incidence of this diagnosis than placebo.
sources.cited_for: The trial establishes that prevention can reduce disease in a defined high-risk population.
sources.not_established: Treatment began before disease developed, so the trial does not establish reversal after onset.

sources.showed: A small pilot used apheresis, a blood-filtering procedure, to remove sFlt-1, a placental protein contributing to maternal illness. Repeated treatment lowered this protein and blood pressure.
sources.quote: Compared to antenatal estimated birth weights, neonatal birth weights generally remained stable or increased among those with the longest extensions.
sources.cited_for: The pilot demonstrates targeted protein removal and accompanying blood-pressure changes.
sources.not_established: Without a comparison group, the pilot cannot establish that treatment delayed delivery or restored placental support.

shown: Thadhani and colleagues tested targeted blood filtering in very early preeclampsia. The repeated-treatment group included nine women. The pilot focused on safety and tolerability; it has not demonstrated recovery sufficient to remove the need for early delivery.
missing: Treatment must restore sustained placental support and fetal growth after disease begins, while resolving maternal illness where present.
Controlled trials must establish that continuing pregnancy reduces serious prematurity without unacceptable harm to mother or baby.

milestones.label: Placental recovery removes the need for early delivery
milestones.explanation: A controlled trial would have to show sustained placental and fetal growth recovery, maternal recovery where needed, and continuation to a less premature stage. This would establish reversal in the pregnancies studied.

milestones.label: Numerical success targets and safety limits are set beforehand
milestones.explanation: Trials would need numerical outcome targets, safety limits, emergency delivery rules, follow-up plans and enough participants set before testing. These would distinguish meaningful recovery from small changes in blood tests or pressure.

milestones.label: Independent studies confirm benefit and safe treatment schedules
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to confirm benefit, identify who responds and establish safe schedules, with follow-up of mothers and children. This would define where treatment works and whether benefits last.

uncertain: Which forms and stages of placental damage remain reversible, and can maternal recovery and fetal growth improve together?
The pregnancy-duration targets, definitions of recovery and acceptable safety margins still need to be specified.
Whether reversal would improve long-term child health or reduce mothers' later cardiovascular disease remains unknown.

page.title: Reversal of placental insufficiency in utero
page.definition: Treatment restores placental oxygen and nutrient supply after insufficiency develops, sustaining fetal growth without disease-driven preterm delivery. For early preeclampsia, a pregnancy disorder involving hypertension and organ or placental dysfunction, it also resolves the maternal syndrome while pregnancy continues.

goal.need: Delivery ends dependence on the placenta but can require birth before fetal maturation. The 2023 reviews identify it as the only definitive treatment for preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction. WHO’s global estimates below quantify the broader burden; they do not isolate early placental disease.

figures.caption: Global burden reported by WHO on 6 October 2026.
figures.note: The death estimate includes hypertensive disorders other than preeclampsia.

statements.quote: to improve fetal growth in severe early onset FGR.
statements.context: The consortium’s final report states this purpose for translating a maternal gene therapy into clinical use. FGR means fetal growth restriction.

statements.quote: Ongoing research addressing causative pathways has the potential to identify new biomarkers and novel therapeutics that target fundamental mechanisms of preeclampsia.

statements.body: International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology
statements.quote: Ultimately, delivery represents the only therapeutic option in early FGR
statements.context: The guideline describes the balance between fetal injury from placental insufficiency and harm from prematurity.

completion.title: Treatment reverses established placental disease and removes its indication for preterm delivery.
completion.criterion: In pregnancies with established placental insufficiency, a randomized controlled trial demonstrates recovery of placental support and fetal growth that removes the disease indication for delivery before 37 weeks. Where preeclampsia is present, maternal hypertension and organ dysfunction also resolve before delivery. Recovery persists through the remainder of pregnancy. The trial must meet prespecified maternal, fetal and neonatal safety criteria. Achievement applies only to the studied disease subgroup.
completion.set_by: Atlas working definition; no outside body’s published antenatal-reversal test was identified.
completion.basis: Searches of FDA/EMA material, SMFM/ISUOG guidance, EVERREST and PI trial protocols found no adopted test of antenatal reversal. Existing protocols test pregnancy duration or infant outcomes. This criterion uses the field’s definition of preterm delivery as before 37 weeks and requires recovery beyond those intermediate benefits. Universal recovery-duration and safety margins remain undefined.

milestones.title: A treatment increases fetal growth in an animal model of placental insufficiency.
milestones.criterion: A controlled animal experiment demonstrates increased fetal growth, EVERREST’s proof-of-principle bar. In the study published on 4 March 2014, 45 sheep pregnancies modelling growth restriction received VEGF gene therapy (18), control vector (14) or saline (13); 12 normally growing pregnancies provided a reference. Ultrasound growth velocity increased at 3–4 weeks after treatment, P=0.016–0.047. Mean fetal weight and uterine blood flow did not significantly increase. This experiment does not establish recovery of the maternal preeclampsia syndrome.
milestones.set_by: EVERREST consortium’s published translational programme; this proof-of-principle criterion was written for placental fetal growth restriction.
milestones.threshold_quote: uterine artery injection of Ad.VEGF-A165 improves fetal growth.

milestones.title: Nonclinical results support starting a pregnancy trial of a placental-disease treatment.
milestones.criterion: Animal or in-vitro pharmacology and toxicology support a conclusion that the proposed clinical investigation is reasonably safe, including relevant reproductive and fetal toxicity evidence. EVERREST’s report, updated on 7 June 2019, describes Good Laboratory Practice reproductive toxicology with no detected fetal vector transfer or harm. The animal sample size is not stated. This programme report supplies preclinical evidence rather than an FDA clearance decision.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.23(a)(8), the nonclinical evidence requirement for an investigational new drug application.
milestones.threshold_quote: it is reasonably safe to conduct the proposed clinical investigations.

milestones.title: Pregnant patients with established placental disease receive treatment in an early-phase study.
milestones.criterion: An early-phase protocol administers treatment after diagnosis during pregnancy and assesses maternal and fetal safety. Preeclampsia: the pilot published on 27 April 2026 treated 7 single-dose and 9 repeated-dose participants. In the latter cohort, each apheresis reduced circulating sFlt-1, a placental protein implicated in maternal disease, by 16.7±7.6%; median admission-to-delivery time was 10 days, without a randomized comparator. Placental FGR: on 12 November 2026, DiaMedica reported 12 participants treated with DM199; this sponsor report is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Thadhani and colleagues’ selective sFlt-1 apheresis pilot protocol; the cited protocol concerns very preterm preeclampsia.
milestones.threshold_quote: then conducted a single-arm, open-label trial to reduce circulating sFlt-1 in women with very preterm preeclampsia.

milestones.title: A randomized trial shows pregnancy prolongation after treatment of placental disease at α=0.05.
milestones.criterion: Randomized superiority on time from randomization to birth, using PI4’s intention-to-treat analysis at α=0.05. Preeclampsia: PI2 randomized 180 women; among 179 analyzed, median durations were 17.7 versus 10.1 days, geometric mean ratio 1.39 (95% CI 0.99–1.95), P=0.057; first published on 22 September 2021. Placental FGR: UK STRIDER randomized 135 women; median durations were 17 versus 18 days, P=0.23; published on 7 December 2017. Neither primary analysis demonstrated superiority.
milestones.set_by: PI4 steering committee, published protocol NCT06033131, for preeclampsia at 22 weeks 0 days–33 weeks 6 days; UK STRIDER independently used pregnancy duration for placental fetal growth restriction.
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary outcome is prolongation of gestation, defined as the time in hours from randomisation to birth.

milestones.title: Treatment reduces perinatal death or major neonatal morbidity in placental disease, with P<0.05.
milestones.criterion: Randomized superiority at two-sided P<0.05 for perinatal death or major neonatal morbidity through discharge. Morbidity comprises intraventricular haemorrhage grade ≥3, periventricular leukomalacia grade ≥2, moderate/severe bronchopulmonary dysplasia, necrotizing enterocolitis Bell stage ≥2, or retinopathy requiring laser treatment. FGR: Dutch STRIDER randomized 216 pregnancies; events occurred in 65/108 versus 58/107, P=0.38; neonatal pulmonary hypertension increased. Published on 17 June 2020. Preeclampsia: PI2 did not show differences in its maternal, fetal or neonatal composites.
milestones.set_by: Dutch STRIDER investigators, registered protocol NCT02277132 and published statistical analysis; this composite was defined for severe early-onset fetal growth restriction.
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary outcome was a composite of perinatal mortality or major neonatal morbidity until hospital discharge.

not_found: The selective sFlt-1 apheresis pilot’s supplementary protocol could not be opened.
The EVERREST final report did not state the animal sample size for its Good Laboratory Practice reproductive toxicology study.

results.detail: Fetal weight distributions suggest improvement, but the supplied text does not report the magnitude or statistical significance of the individual fetal-weight difference. Increased total litter weight in the other model may reflect changes in litter size.

results.finding: Angiotensinogen-targeting siRNA improved fetal growth restriction in 2 rodent models of preeclampsia; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The supplied text reports improved growth but gives no quantitative fetal-growth result, sample size, or description of a control group, so the controlled-experiment criterion cannot be established from it.
results.quote: siRNA treatment ameliorated the preeclamptic phenotype in both models, reduced blood pressure, and improved intrauterine growth restriction, with no observed deleterious effects on the fetus.

results.finding: In guinea pigs with placental insufficiency, IGF1 treatment increased directly treated male fetal weight versus sham (5 treated and 6 sham dams; P=0.036).
results.detail: Treatment began after growth restriction was established. Only male fetuses received direct treatment; indirectly exposed fetuses did not differ significantly in weight from sham-treated animals.

results.finding: In 45 growth-restricted sheep pregnancies, VEGF gene therapy increased fetal growth velocity at 3–4 weeks (P=0.016–0.047).
results.detail: The randomized experiment compared 18 treated pregnancies with 27 receiving control vector or saline; 12 normal pregnancies provided a reference. Mean fetal weight and uterine blood flow did not significantly increase.
results.quote: In summary, midgestation delivery of Ad.VEGF gene therapy in FGR pregnancy induced by overnourishment of adolescent sheep dams resulted in a significant increase in fetal growth velocity at 3 and 4 weeks posttreatment.

results.finding: DM199 reproductive toxicology: sample size not stated; no adverse developmental, offspring or fertility effects reported in 2 animal species.
results.detail: The protocol also reports tolerability at doses 20-fold above expected human therapeutic doses and undetectable fetal blood concentrations in rats. The underlying animal study details and sample sizes are not stated.
results.quote: Reproductive toxicology studies in two animal species have been completed using DM199 doses that are significantly higher than the proportionate dosing planned for humans. These studies showed no adverse effects on fetal development, offspring (followed for two generations) or future fertility.

results.finding: EVERREST VEGF gene therapy: animal sample size not stated; no fetal vector transfer or harm detected.
results.detail: The GLP reproductive toxicology study used the clinical vector and informed the proposed trial dose. The report does not state the animal sample size or report trial clearance.
results.quote: These showed no evidence that the vector crossed the placenta to the fetus in the pre-clinical animal model, and that there was no evidence of harm.

results.finding: TADAFER II assessed safety in 44 tadalafil-treated pregnancies with fetal growth restriction.
results.detail: Treatment followed an FGR diagnosis, and maternal and fetal or neonatal safety were assessed. The trial did not require or establish a placental cause of FGR; some participants had abnormal Doppler findings.
results.quote: We included 44 cases in the tadalafil treatment group and 43 cases in the conventional treatment group in the safety analysis.

results.finding: In 100 pregnancies with preeclampsia, sildenafil prolonged pregnancy versus placebo (P=.008).
results.detail: This randomized trial reports a significant difference in time to delivery, but it is not the specified PI4 intention-to-treat analysis.
results.quote: Pregnancy duration was on average 4 days longer (14.4 days, 95% confidence interval [CI] 12.5-16.6 days compared with 10.4 days, 95% CI 8.4-12.3 days, P=.008) and percent reduction in pulsatility indices of uterine and umbilical arteries higher (22.5% and 18.5%, compared with placebo 2.1% and 2.5%, P<.001) for patients treated with sildenafil compared with placebo.

results.finding: Early-onset FGR trial (n=40): interval to delivery was longer with treatment (P=0.048).
results.detail: The trial reports mean intervals of 37.8 versus 27.1 days. It does not specify that the interval ran from randomization to birth or that the analysis used PI4’s intention-to-treat approach.
results.quote:
Table
3
demonstrated that Group A had more favorable outcomes in terms of later gestational age at delivery, increased delivery interval, neonatal birth weight, APGAR scores, lower NICU admission rates, and less deterioration in Doppler indices, with statistically significant P values of 0.018, 0.048,0.041,0.003, 0.01, 0.026, and 0.026, respectively.

results.finding: In 7 women with preterm preeclampsia, maternal and fetal vital signs remained stable during single-dose apheresis.
results.detail: The pilot also treated 9 women in a multiple-dose cohort. Safety and tolerability were the primary endpoints.
results.quote:
In women with preterm preeclampsia treated with single ascending doses (phase A,
n
= 7, preapheresis, mean ± s.d., sFlt-1: 15,120 ± 4,484 pg ml
−1
), maternal and fetal vital signs and umbilical artery pulsatility indices remained stable when comparing measures before, during and after apheresis.

results.finding: In 9 treated and 16 untreated women, the reported time-to-delivery hazard ratio was 0.14.
results.detail: The comparison was not randomized, so it does not satisfy the randomized superiority criterion.
results.quote: Kaplan-Meier survival curve showing time to delivery is depicted for treated (N = 9 in Phase B) and untreated women (N = 16) (Hazard ratio 0.14, 95% CI 0.04–0.50, P = 0.0003).

results.finding: VEGF mRNA LNP 55 alleviated hypertension in an inflammation-induced preeclampsia model; n=8 mice per group.
results.detail: The study provides animal pharmacology and limited safety observations, but does not establish sufficient reproductive and fetal toxicology to support the reasonable safety of a pregnancy trial.
results.quote: A single injection of VEGF mRNA LNP 55 immediately and permanently alleviated maternal hypertension in pre-eclamptic mice until the end of gestation.

results.finding: In 2 rodent models, Agt-targeting siRNA improved the preeclamptic phenotype without observed fetal harm; animal sample size was not stated.
results.detail: The study provides nonclinical pharmacology and fetal observations, but the supplied text does not establish a sufficient reproductive and fetal toxicology assessment to support starting a pregnancy trial.
results.quote: siRNA treatment ameliorated the preeclamptic phenotype in both models, reduced blood pressure, and improved intrauterine growth restriction, with no observed deleterious effects on the fetus.

results.finding: In 5 treated guinea pig pregnancies, repeated placental IGF1 treatment caused no observed fetal loss.
results.detail: The study reports maternal and fetal observations alongside pharmacological effects, but it does not establish the reproductive and fetal toxicology evidence needed to support a pregnancy trial.
results.quote:
Repeated nanoparticle-mediated
IGF1
treatments from mid pregnancy to near term resulted in no maternal health complications, no fetal loss, and no placental hemorrhage.

results.finding: In 57 sheep pregnancies, all fetuses remained viable until necropsy at 131±0.2 days.
results.detail: The study reports maternal and fetal observations alongside pharmacology, but does not establish the reproductive and fetal toxicology evidence needed to support clinical investigation. Full reproductive toxicology studies were planned.
results.quote: All pregnancies remained viable until the point of necropsy at 131±0.2 days of gestation and no maternal health problems were observed.

results.finding: In 79 analyzed pregnancies, tadalafil did not significantly prolong gestation: P=0.11.
results.detail: The secondary analysis measured time from treatment to birth and excluded intrauterine fetal deaths; it was not the required intention-to-treat analysis from randomization. Significant subgroup results were post hoc.

results.finding: Among 87 pregnancies in the safety analysis, fetal, neonatal and infant deaths were 1/44 versus 7/43, P=0.03.
results.detail: The significant total includes infant deaths beyond the criterion's perinatal endpoint. The study did not report superiority for the specified perinatal death or major neonatal morbidity composite.
results.quote:
The most important result of this safety evaluation study is the significant decrease in fetal, neonatal, and infantile deaths in the tadalafil group to the conventional treatment group: 1/44 (2%) vs. 7/43 (16%), respectively (
p
= 0.03).

results.finding: In 100 pregnancies with preeclampsia, 50 patients were randomized to sildenafil.
results.detail: The trial treated diagnosed patients during pregnancy and assessed maternal complications and adverse neonatal outcomes. The supplied text does not identify it as an early-phase study.
results.quote: In a randomized double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 100 singleton pregnancies with preeclampsia between 24 and 33 weeks of gestation were randomized to 50 mg oral sildenafil citrate every 8 hours or placebo.

results.finding: In 100 pregnancies with preeclampsia, there was no difference in perinatal morbidity or mortality between groups.
results.detail: The text reports no difference and does not specify the milestone’s neonatal morbidity composite or a P value for it.
results.quote: There was no difference in perinatal morbidity, mortality, or adverse effects between groups.

results.finding: In a randomized study of 40 pregnancies with early-onset FGR, 20 received nitroglycerin and increased oral fluid intake.
results.detail: Treatment followed diagnosis, and maternal side effects and fetal outcomes were assessed. The paper does not identify the trial as early phase.
results.quote: A total of 40 pregnant women diagnosed with early onset FGR were recruited from Ain Shams University Maternity Hospital between June 2023 to December 2023. The patients were randomly assigned into two groups, 20 in each group.

results.finding: Among 40 pregnancies with early-onset FGR, neonatal death did not differ significantly between treatment and control groups (P=0.375).
results.detail: The randomized trial reported neonatal deaths and intrauterine fetal deaths separately; it did not demonstrate superiority for the specified perinatal death or major neonatal morbidity outcome.
results.quote: Conversely, there were no statistically significant difference regarding the mode of delivery, incidence of IUFD, fetal distress, and neonatal death with P values 0.16, 0.151, 0.102, and 0.375, respectively.

results.finding: In a rat model of preeclampsia, etanercept increased fetal weight versus vehicle (8 dams per group; p=0.0480).
results.detail: Fetal survival remained reduced, and placental morphology and nutrient transporter expression did not improve. The study does not establish resolution of the maternal syndrome.
results.quote: Average fetal weight per dam was significantly increased in viable offspring from Etan-RUPP compared to RUPP (p=0.0480)

results.finding: Severe preeclampsia: 133 women randomized; gestation was prolonged with antithrombin (P=0.007).
results.detail: The source reports significant gestational prolongation but does not establish superiority on time from randomization to birth using PI4’s intention-to-treat analysis.
results.quote: Gestation was significantly prolonged (p = 0.007), and the number of low-birth weight infants was significantly smaller (p = 0.011) in the AT group.

results.finding: KOUNO-TORI: 181 women analyzed; antithrombin versus placebo for pregnancy prolongation, P=0.07.
results.detail: The randomized trial did not demonstrate superiority at α=0.05. Its endpoint was time from treatment initiation to delivery, and its full analysis set excluded two randomized women who did not receive treatment; it was not PI4’s intention-to-treat analysis.
results.quote:
There was no statistically significant difference in the pregnancy period between the placebo and rhAT-gamma groups (
P
=0.07).
